reminder.notes:
The alarm's buttons answer instantly now

On one phone, tapping Complete on a ringing alarm did nothing for twenty seconds. The action was
never lost -- the reminder was completed and saved within milliseconds -- but the full-screen alert
stayed on screen, unchanged, until a wait none of it depended on finally gave up. Twenty seconds of
a screen that does not react is indistinguishable from a broken button.

The wait was for a Firebase session. Closing the alarm was queued behind resolving one, so it could
mirror the action to the other phone through the cloud. On a device whose alarm engine cannot
restore that session at all -- which the diagnostics had already proven, and which is exactly why
the Wi-Fi lane was built -- the wait could only ever end in a timeout, and the app spent it twice:
once at ring time, then again from scratch the moment the button was pressed.

### Bug fixes

- Complete, Dismiss and Snooze now close the alarm as soon as the action is applied. Closing is
  capped at two seconds, whatever is still running behind it, so the alert can never sit there
  looking dead.
- A Firebase session that has already failed to resolve is no longer asked for a second time when
  you act. That second lookup was the twenty seconds.
- Giving up on the cloud handshake is safe here: both phones work out the same winner
  independently, by design.

### Features

- The Wi-Fi broadcast now leaves before anything touches your account, so the other phone stops
  ringing at once instead of after a wait it never needed.
- The buttons acknowledge themselves. The one you press shows a spinner and the rest go inert the
  instant you touch them, so even slow work reads as work in progress rather than as nothing
  happening.

Still not fixed: that phone cannot keep a Firebase session alive for its alarm engine. It is routed
around, not solved.

cards.notes:
Cards 2.5.0 — Background update checks, and no more double-downloading updates

### Features
- Cards now checks for updates periodically in the background (about every 6 hours) and posts a notification when one is found, in addition to the existing manual "Check for Updates" in Settings. Tapping the notification opens the app; the download and install still happen from the Settings sheet.

### Bug fixes
- The update downloader now persists its in-flight DownloadManager id and re-attaches to a still-running download instead of deleting the partial file and starting over — fixes re-downloading the same update from zero after backgrounding or reopening the app mid-update.
- The update sheet now re-syncs its progress on resume instead of occasionally showing a frozen progress bar.

mirrordrive.notes:
Show the app version and PNSJY branding in Settings

No user-facing bug fixes in this release.

localsender.notes:
Local Sender 1.0.11 - security hardening (full audit)

A full security audit (see AUDIT.md and THREAT_MODEL.md in the repo) and fixes for
every CRITICAL and HIGH finding it turned up. All local content is now encrypted
at rest, the macOS build is sandboxed again, and Drive backup no longer stores its
own key next to the data it protects.

### Features
- Google Drive backup is now sealed with a passphrase you set and never upload —
  Drive alone can no longer read a backup, only you can.
- A warning dialog when a device presents a different identity key than the one
  already trusted under that name, instead of an ordinary pairing prompt.

### Bug fixes
- Chat history, rooms, trusted-peer keys, peer profiles, network profiles, and
  device name are now encrypted at rest (previously plaintext in local storage).
- Fixed a path-traversal bug where an incoming file offer's name could write
  outside the downloads folder.
- Fixed an unbounded network frame length that let any device on the LAN push
  memory usage toward the app's limit with a single unauthenticated connection.
- A silent, unresponsive peer during pairing could lock the app out of pairing
  with anyone else; pairing now times out and recovers.
- A connection dropped mid-file-transfer no longer leaves a frozen progress row
  or an orphaned partial file on disk.
- Re-enabled the macOS App Sandbox (previously off since v1.0.1 to work around a
  Keychain hang); the underlying hang is now handled by an existing timeout and
  fallback, so sandboxing no longer breaks pairing.
- The identity key's on-disk fallback file (used only when the OS secure store is
  unavailable) is now encrypted instead of holding the raw key.

bchat.notes:
BChat 0.1.0-beta.4 — plain language and fewer things to figure out

This release is about making the app usable by someone who has never heard of a mesh network. The
app used to name things the way the protocol underneath it does; now it names them the way a person
would, and the two places where you had to know how it worked before you could use it are gone.

### Features
- Everything is said in plain words. No links, relays, mesh, handshakes, advertising, fingerprints
  or hops in anything you read. The Nearby room is now Everyone nearby, "3 direct links" is
  "Connected to 3 phones near you", and a relayed message says it arrived via 2 phones
- Tapping someone in Nearby opens the chat and sets up the secure connection on the way in, instead
  of leaving the row doing nothing until you found the Connect button
- Settings leads with your profile, Stay reachable and Battery use, in words that say what they do.
  The Bluetooth readout and the diagnostics log moved to Settings, Advanced, where they are still
  one tap away when something needs reporting
- The safety number is now called a safety code, and the screen explains what comparing it protects
  you from

### Bug fixes
- A chat you started was titled with the other person's 64-character key instead of their name. It
  is now named after the person, and a chat created before they were identified is renamed as soon
  as they are
- Search results and starred messages showed that same key as the subtitle instead of the chat name

### Known limits
- Photos, voice notes, groups, file transfer and the Wi-Fi LAN transport are still not in this
  build.
- Multi-hop relay remains verified in simulation only; it needs a third device.
- Verified by 120 unit tests and an emulator run, not on the two phones.
- iOS is not built yet.
